question: When taking a rheumatologic history from a patient with polyarthritis, which historical feature is MOST useful in differentiating rheumatoid arthritis from psoriatic arthritis?

answers.text: Duration of morning stiffness greater than one hour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prolonged morning stiffness is a feature of both RA and psoriatic arthritis (PsA), both being inflammatory polyarthritides. It does not reliably differentiate the two.

answers.text: Presence of skin plaques, nail pitting, or dactylitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Psoriatic plaques, nail changes (pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis), and dactylitis ('sausage digit') are specific features of psoriatic arthritis not seen in RA. A careful skin and nail examination is therefore part of every rheumatologic history and examination.

answers.text: Symmetric involvement of small joints of the hands and wrists

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Symmetric small-joint polyarthritis of the hands and wrists is the classic presentation of RA but can also occur in the polyarticular form of psoriatic arthritis. It does not differentiate the two conditions reliably.
Elevated ESR is a non-specific marker of inflammation present in both RA and PsA. It does not differentiate the two.

overallFeedback.feedback: When differentiating RA from psoriatic arthritis, look for the psoriatic spectrum: skin plaques, nail pitting/onycholysis, dactylitis, and axial involvement (sacroiliitis). Up to 30% of PsA patients have skin disease that follows rather than precedes joint disease — so always ask specifically about psoriasis in family members too.
Well done. Psoriasis-related cutaneous and nail features (plaques, pitting, dactylitis) are the key differentiating historical and examination findings in psoriatic arthritis versus RA.
